Longitudinal Summary

Across 2023, management framed revenue growth as driven by Parks, Experiences, and Products (with both revenue and operating income increasing by more than 10% versus the prior year) while noting mixed trends in certain segments such as Domestic Linear Networks affiliate revenue (down 2% due to subscriber declines, partially offset by rate increases). In Q4 2023 (fiscal 2022 results presented), Disney reported double-digit growth in service revenues and cited specific drivers such as higher theme park and resort revenues and subscription revenue growth. By Q3 2024, management explicitly highlighted that Q3 revenue growth was only 2%. For fiscal 2024 (reported in Q4 2024), the company reported overall revenues up 3% to $91.4 billion, and revenues service revenues up 3% to $81.8 billion, indicating a slower growth profile versus the stronger 2023 narrative and earlier disclosed fiscal growth rates.

Forecasting Credibility: None

No guidance/actual pairs specific to the topic of revenue growth were provided in the evidence, so forecasting credibility cannot be assessed. While management commentary described revenue growth drivers (e.g., Parks, Experiences, and Products and Q3 2% revenue growth), there is no comparable forward guidance figure for revenue growth to validate against subsequent results.

Trends

  • 2023 commentary suggests stronger revenue growth at Parks, Experiences, and Products (more than 10% vs. prior year)
  • Mixed segment performance in 2023 (Domestic Linear Networks affiliate revenue down 2% despite contractual rate increases)
  • Revenue growth moderated by Q3 2024 (explicitly stated as 2%)
  • Fiscal 2024 overall revenue growth was modest (up 3% to $91.4 billion; service revenues up 3% to $81.8 billion)

Recurring Themes / Risks

  • Segment-level mix effects (affiliate subscriber trends vs. contractual rate increases)
  • Revenue growth tied to subscription and parks/experiences performance
  • Execution and external conditions impacting growth and profitability (general risk language)
  • Florida legislative/regulatory steps flagged as potentially negatively impacting growth/profitability (not quantified here)

Key Concerns

  • Guidance/actual evidence for revenue growth is not available for a credibility assessment (no guidance-vs-actual pair count provided for this topic).
  • Growth appears to decelerate over time in the evidence (explicitly 2% in Q3 2024; 3% for fiscal 2024), which may indicate underlying demand/segment normalization, but the provided excerpts do not show a single consistent bridge from quarter-by-quarter guidance to results.
  • Potential topical risk from Florida legislation/regulatory steps could affect growth, but the provided excerpts do not quantify the impact on revenue.

Conclusion

Revenue growth evolved from a 2023 narrative emphasizing stronger contribution from Parks, Experiences, and Products (revenue and operating income increasing by more than 10% vs. the prior year) and specific upsides in theme parks (e.g., higher admissions components and merchandise/food/beverage volume and spend) to a more moderate growth profile later. In Q3 2024, management stated the company had 2% revenue growth. For fiscal 2024, the company reported revenues increasing 3% to $91.4 billion, and revenues service revenues increasing 3% to $81.8 billion. Overall, the evidence supports that revenue growth remained positive throughout, but decelerated by the later period.

Thank you. I'm going to try to squeeze in two, one on theme parks and one on NBA. So first on theme parks, there's really a lot of moving pieces here. Can you provide color on global park demand and where you expect this protracted weakness? Maybe include the benefit from cruise ships since you have three ships coming on over the next, I guess, 18 months or so. And with the stated fiscal Q4 mid-single-digit decline and the expectation that this will last for several quarters, is that the right level to think about OI as we think about fiscal '25? And on the NBA, with the rights now complete, you'll likely have several hundred million dollar step up when the new contract begins in fiscal '26. Are there incremental monetization drivers, including maybe WNBA growth, that can make the new contract profitable in the early years? Thank you.Q3 2024complete1Earnings transcripthighsource
Great. Thanks, Jessica. This is Hugh. That was a six-part first question, so I'll try to answer it as best I can. First, just to sort of peel apart Q3, again, I want to emphasize we actually had 2% revenue growth in Q3. The reason obviously is the IP is so strong in our parks. It really does attract a strong audience, and people are reluctant to cancel vacations. So while we saw a slight moderation in demand, I certainly wouldn't call it a significant change. That said, 40% of the Experiences business is actually not domestic parks. It's either international parks or consumer products, and that's from an operating income perspective. 60% is domestic parks, including cruise ships. Within that, we saw attendance flat in the quarter, and we saw per caps up a little bit. We expect to see a flattish revenue number in Q4 coming out of the parks. And as we mentioned in -- earlier in the letter, really just a few quarters. So I don't think I'd refer to it as protracted, but just a couple of quarters of likely similar results. Now keep in mind, we do have some expenses attached to our ships coming in, and that will affect us a bit in '24 and a bit in '25. But overall, I would just call this as a bit of a slowdown that's being more than offset by the Entertainment business, both what we've seen so far and our expectations for Moana 2 as well as Mufasa.Q3 2024complete1Earnings transcripthighsource

Q3 2023
View TranscriptView SEC filing

What management said

  • "Growth in addressable revenue increased, representing over 40% of the total upfront volume, and sports pricing is up single digits across the board."
  • "Our Parks, Experiences, and Products portfolio of businesses continues to be an earnings and free cash flow growth driver for the company with both revenue and operating income increasing by more than 10% versus the prior year."
  • "Domestic Linear Networks affiliate revenue decreased by 2% from the prior year due to a 6-point decline from fewer subscribers, partially offset by 4 points of growth from contractual rate increases."
  • "These factors include economic or industry conditions; competition and execution risks, including in connection with our business plans, organizational structure, and operating changes; cost savings; earnings expectations; and drivers of growth; and our DTC content and how it's made available on our platform; subscriber; advertising; and revenue growth and profitability; in particular, our expectations regarding DTC profitability are built on certain assumptions around subscriber additions based on the availability and attractiveness of our future content, which is subject to additional risks related to ongoing work stoppages; churn expectations; the financial impact of the Disney+ ad tier and price increases; our ability to quickly execute on cost rationalization while preserving revenue and macroeconomic conditions, all of which, while based on extensive internal analysis as well as our recent experience, provide a layer of uncertainty in our outlook."
  • "International parks continued its strong growth trend with year-over-year operating income increasing at all our international sites, but most significantly at Shanghai Disney, which saw record highs from a revenue, OI, and margin perspective."
  • "Our Cruise Line in particular showed strong revenue and operating income growth in the third quarter."

What was asked

Q — Michael Morris — Guggenheim: Thank you very much. Good afternoon, guys. So on the theme of considering options for Disney, there was an article published recently that speculated that the entire company could be sold to a larger technology company. So Bob, my straightforward question is, do you see a plausible scenario where the entire company would be sold? Maybe a bit more broadly, though, when you think of maximum value of the Disney enterprise, do you think that can be achieved by being more aligned with a single technology partner? Or is that value maximized through partnering with a variety of tech platforms? And if I could just sneak one in on the Penn Gaming announcement. Does it -- will you forego advertising partnerships with all other betting or sports gaming partners? And if so, how much impact will that have in exchange for building value in this partnership?
A: I -- Michael, I just am not going to speculate about the potential for Disney to be acquired by any company, whether a technology company or not. Obviously, anyone who want to speculate about these things would have to immediately consider the global regulatory environment. I'll say no more than that. It's just -- it's not something that we obsess about. Great. And then, Michael, with respect to any foregone economics or no longer accepting advertising from other gaming companies, I don't see us in a position where we'll ever be in that situation. OK. Thanks for the question, and I want to thank everyone for joining us today. Note that a reconciliation of our non-GAAP measures that were referred to on this call to equivalent GAAP measures can be found on our Investor Relations website. Let me also remind you that certain statements on this call, including financial estimates or statements about our plans, guidance or expectations, or other statements that are not historical in nature may constitute forward-looking statements under the securities laws. We make these statements on the basis of our views and assumptions regarding future events and business performance at the time that we make them, and we do not undertake any obligation to update these statements. Forward-looking statements are subject to a number of risks and uncertainties, and actual results may differ materially from the results expressed or implied in light of a variety of factors. These factors include economic or industry conditions; competition and execution risks, including in connection with our business plans, organizational structure, and operating changes; cost savings; earnings expectations; and drivers of growth; and our DTC content and how it's made available on our platform; subscriber; advertising; and revenue growth and profitability; in particular, our expectations regarding DTC profitability are built on certain assumptions around subscriber additions based on the availability and attractiveness of our future content, which is subject to additional risks related to ongoing work stoppages; churn expectations; the financial impact of the Disney+ ad tier and price increases; our ability to quickly execute on cost rationalization while preserving revenue and macroeconomic conditions, all of which, while based on extensive internal analysis as well as our recent experience, provide a layer of uncertainty in our outlook. For more information about key risk factors, please refer to our Investor Relations website, the press release issued today risks and uncertainties described in our Form 10-K, Form 10-Q, and other filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. We want to thank you all for joining us and wish everyone a good rest of the day.

What was asked

Q — Jessica Reif Ehrlich — Bank of America: Thank you. I'm going to try to squeeze in two, one on theme parks and one on NBA. So first on theme parks, there's really a lot of moving pieces here. Can you provide color on global park demand and where you expect this protracted weakness? Maybe include the benefit from cruise ships since you have three ships coming on over the next, I guess, 18 months or so. And with the stated fiscal Q4 mid-single-digit decline and the expectation that this will last for several quarters, is that the right level to think about OI as we think about fiscal '25? And on the NBA, with the rights now complete, you'll likely have several hundred million dollar step up when the new contract begins in fiscal '26. Are there incremental monetization drivers, including maybe WNBA growth, that can make the new contract profitable in the early years? Thank you.
A: Great. Thanks, Jessica. This is Hugh. That was a six-part first question, so I'll try to answer it as best I can. First, just to sort of peel apart Q3, again, I want to emphasize we actually had 2% revenue growth in Q3. The reason obviously is the IP is so strong in our parks. It really does attract a strong audience, and people are reluctant to cancel vacations. So while we saw a slight moderation in demand, I certainly wouldn't call it a significant change. That said, 40% of the Experiences business is actually not domestic parks. It's either international parks or consumer products, and that's from an operating income perspective. 60% is domestic parks, including cruise ships. Within that, we saw attendance flat in the quarter, and we saw per caps up a little bit. We expect to see a flattish revenue number in Q4 coming out of the parks. And as we mentioned in -- earlier in the letter, really just a few quarters. So I don't think I'd refer to it as protracted, but just a couple of quarters of likely similar results. Now keep in mind, we do have some expenses attached to our ships coming in, and that will affect us a bit in '24 and a bit in '25. But overall, I would just call this as a bit of a slowdown that's being more than offset by the Entertainment business, both what we've seen so far and our expectations for Moana 2 as well as Mufasa. Regarding the NBA deal, Jessica, first of all, let me just remind you and everyone that the deal doesn't kick in next year. It's a year later. We have one more year on the current deal. And as we looked at it, first of all, one goal was to maintain what we call the A package, which means we've got the finals for 11 more years or now we have the finals for 12 years, and they drive significant value for us. Also, overall, the deal reflects the value of live programming. We know that that's been an advertiser's delight and also an audience delight. It also reflects the growing value of basketball and the growing value of women's sports as a large WNBA component to this. Also as part of this deal and has been the strategy of ESPN for a while to lock in sports rights for a long period of time, it secures our ability to bring ESPN in the digital direction, particularly as we look to launch flagship sometime at the end of 2025. And so we believe that by the time this kicks in a year from now that a lot of the pieces will be in place in terms of driving more advertising revenue, more distribution revenue moving to digital. And another thing that we've done here is we've secured international rights, particularly to the finals, not in every market around the world, but in most markets. And that will drive some added revenue as well. Not going to be specific about the profitability in the early years, but there's tremendous value in this deal. Thank you. Next question.

Longitudinal Summary

Across the period, management discussed operating margin primarily through segment-level or qualitative comparisons, with recurring references to Parks/Experiences recovery and DTC margin expansion. In Q3 2023, the only forward-looking element related to DPEP operating margins indicated expectations for Q4 2023 to exceed the prior year, but no resolved “guidance vs actual” margin figure is provided in the excerpt to close the loop. In Q2 2024, the guidance is framed as an aspiration for DTC “double-digit operating margin,” while the company simultaneously declined to provide competitors with timing details. By Q4 2024, the filings show operating income/loss movement in DTC and other segments, and disclose a reporting-unit aggregation change for entertainment businesses based on projected long-term operating margins, which can affect comparability of reported “operating margin” measures over time.

Forecasting Credibility: None

No guidance/actual pairs for operating margin were found with enough precision to judge a Met vs Miss pattern. Where management provided margin-related expectations (e.g., DPEP Q4 2023 to exceed prior year; DTC double-digit operating margin aspiration), the provided evidence does not include a corresponding filing-sourced actual margin metric that resolves the guidance in the excerpts, so forecasting credibility cannot be assessed from a guidance-vs-actual comparison count of zero.

Revenue & Operating Income trend
Revenue ($23.51B → $23.16B) Operating Income (% of revenue) (12.9% → 18.2%)
Q1 2023 – Q3 2024
▲ Operating Income turned up in Q3 2024

Trends

  • Margin narrative shifted from Parks/Experiences recovery (Q3 2023) toward DTC operating leverage aspirations (Q2 2024)
  • Segment operating income/loss volatility appears across linear networks (Q4 2023) and DTC turning to positive operating income (FY 2024 disclosure)
  • Reporting structure changed in FY 2024 by aggregating entertainment businesses, potentially impacting how operating margin is presented/comparable

Recurring Themes / Risks

  • Reliance on excluding/adjusting items (e.g., Starcruiser accelerated depreciation) for margin comparisons
  • DTC margin as a strategic goal stated as an aspiration rather than a time-bound target
  • Segment mix and regional performance (e.g., international parks, ESPN/Star) driving margin outcomes
  • Potential comparability risk due to entertainment reporting-unit aggregation

Key Concerns

  • Guidance resolution risk: Q3 2023 provides an expectation for Q4 2023 DPEP operating margins to exceed the prior year, but the provided excerpts do not include the corresponding filing-sourced DPEP operating margin outcome needed for a guidance-vs-actual assessment.
  • DTC margin goal lacks timing specificity: Q2 2024 states an aspiration for double-digit operating margin and declines to provide competitors the pathway/timing, limiting ability to evaluate forecast accuracy.
  • Accounting/reporting comparability: FY 2024 filing excerpt discloses aggregation of entertainment businesses into a single reporting unit based on projected long-term operating margins, which may change how operating margin is measured/presented versus prior reporting.

Conclusion

Operating margin trends are discussed in management commentary through segment recovery (domestic Parks/Experiences down vs prior year in Q3 2023, DPEP slightly higher) and through an aspiration for DTC to reach double-digit operating margin (Q2 2024). However, from the evidence provided, there is insufficient guidance-vs-actual resolution for operating margin to quantify whether margins expanded or contracted relative to stated targets in a way that enables forecasting credibility. Filing excerpts indicate meaningful operating income/loss dynamics around the components that feed operating margin (e.g., Direct-to-Consumer moving from an operating loss of $2,496 million to operating income of $143 million in FY 2024), but a precise, consistently reported operating margin metric for the guidance periods is not provided. Additionally, FY 2024 reporting-unit aggregation for entertainment businesses based on operating margin projections introduces potential comparability constraints when assessing operating margin across time.

Thank you. So first, thanks for that detail on parks and experiences and what you expect in the third quarter. I just wanted to dig into some of those demand comments a little more. So as you start to lap some of the post-COVID rebound, what's your expectation for attendance maybe at the domestic level and at the global level? As you start to exit fiscal '24 and into '25, do you think things will continue to be stable or are any of those softening trends sufficient that you expect attendance to have any kind of year-on-year decline? And then on the DTC side of things, Hugh, I think you've talked about a double-digit operating margin as the aspiration. I was wondering if you could just give us any timing as to when we can expect those types of margins? And maybe you could speak to the underlying performance of DTC excluding Hotstar, since I think you're going to be deconsolidating that next year. Thank you.Q2 2024complete1Earnings transcripthighsource
Great. Good morning, Steve. Happy to weigh in on both of those. First, in terms of attendance, look, what we're basically communicating is relative to the post-COVID highs, things are tending to normalize. The parks business did 10% growth in the quarter. And obviously, that's an extremely high revenue number. That said, we still see in -- the bookings that we look ahead toward indicate healthy growth in the business. So we still certainly feel good about the opportunities for continued strong growth. In addition to that, just to comment a bit more on the timing, as I mentioned on the intro, we do have some one-time expenses occurring in Q3. If we were to back out one-timers both for Q3 and Q4, we expect OI for the quarter to be in the mid-to-high single-digit range for Q3 and to be double-digit for Q4. So I certainly feel like the Parks business is still doing very, very well. Obviously, we've got the best in the business in terms of product. And people still have a strong desire to basically go on vacation and come to see us. With regard to DTC margins, a couple of comments on that. First, our goal with this business is to make it a great growth business with healthy margins. We want both, not one versus the other. We've got a lot of levers that give us strong reasons to believe that there's good growth in front of us, whether it's the great programming we have, whether it's higher engagement through bundling and we've got examples of that coming in Latin America as well as adding the sports tile, the ESPN tile to our Disney+ offering. And obviously, we've already added Hulu. In addition to that, password sharing remains an opportunity we're just getting started on, reducing distribution costs for an opportunity and leveraging technology for direct-to-consumer marketing as well as recommendation engines, which help both on the revenue and cost side. And ultimately, we'll get to building out the international business even more strongly. So from the perspective of building the business, it will be a combination of both managing costs more tightly, but also growth which will allow us to leverage the cost structure we have right now. And we feel very, very positively about that. Specific timing, I'm not going to comment on for margins. I don't like to get ahead of the next year until we get to the next year. And in addition to that, from a competitive perspective, I'd rather not give my competitors the pathway on exactly how we're -- how and when we're going to achieve the margin goals we're looking to achieve. But overall, business is in great shape and we feel good about the growth prospects.Q2 2024complete1Earnings transcripthighsource

What management said

  • "At experiences, second-quarter revenue grew 10%, operating income grew 12% and segment margins expanded by 60 basis points versus the prior year."
  • "At our entertainment segment, second-quarter operating income increased by over 70% versus prior year, driven by direct-to-consumer."
  • "Entertainment DTC revenue increased 2% sequentially and 13% year over year, and generated operating income of $47 million."
  • "And then on the DTC side of things, Hugh, I think you've talked about a double-digit operating margin as the aspiration."
2 guidance point(s)3 distinct actual(s)0 verified outcome(s)

What was asked

Q — Steven Cahall — Wells Fargo: Thank you. So first, thanks for that detail on parks and experiences and what you expect in the third quarter. I just wanted to dig into some of those demand comments a little more. So as you start to lap some of the post-COVID rebound, what's your expectation for attendance maybe at the domestic level and at the global level? As you start to exit fiscal '24 and into '25, do you think things will continue to be stable or are any of those softening trends sufficient that you expect attendance to have any kind of year-on-year decline? And then on the DTC side of things, Hugh, I think you've talked about a double-digit operating margin as the aspiration. I was wondering if you could just give us any timing as to when we can expect those types of margins? And maybe you could speak to the underlying performance of DTC excluding Hotstar, since I think you're going to be deconsolidating that next year. Thank you.
A: Great. Good morning, Steve. Happy to weigh in on both of those. First, in terms of attendance, look, what we're basically communicating is relative to the post-COVID highs, things are tending to normalize. The parks business did 10% growth in the quarter. And obviously, that's an extremely high revenue number. That said, we still see in -- the bookings that we look ahead toward indicate healthy growth in the business. So we still certainly feel good about the opportunities for continued strong growth. In addition to that, just to comment a bit more on the timing, as I mentioned on the intro, we do have some one-time expenses occurring in Q3. If we were to back out one-timers both for Q3 and Q4, we expect OI for the quarter to be in the mid-to-high single-digit range for Q3 and to be double-digit for Q4. So I certainly feel like the Parks business is still doing very, very well. Obviously, we've got the best in the business in terms of product. And people still have a strong desire to basically go on vacation and come to see us. With regard to DTC margins, a couple of comments on that. First, our goal with this business is to make it a great growth business with healthy margins. We want both, not one versus the other. We've got a lot of levers that give us strong reasons to believe that there's good growth in front of us, whether it's the great programming we have, whether it's higher engagement through bundling and we've got examples of that coming in Latin America as well as adding the sports tile, the ESPN tile to our Disney+ offering. And obviously, we've already added Hulu. In addition to that, password sharing remains an opportunity we're just getting started on, reducing distribution costs for an opportunity and leveraging technology for direct-to-consumer marketing as well as recommendation engines, which help both on the revenue and cost side. And ultimately, we'll get to building out the international business even more strongly. So from the perspective of building the business, it will be a combination of both managing costs more tightly, but also growth which will allow us to leverage the cost structure we have right now. And we feel very, very positively about that. Specific timing, I'm not going to comment on for margins. I don't like to get ahead of the next year until we get to the next year. And in addition to that, from a competitive perspective, I'd rather not give my competitors the pathway on exactly how we're -- how and when we're going to achieve the margin goals we're looking to achieve. But overall, business is in great shape and we feel good about the growth prospects. Operator, next question, please.
